articles.title: Rugby League World Cup 2030 to be staged in Pacific-USA with eligibility rules updated and Tonga, Samoa given Tier 1 status
articles.summary: It has been proposed that Tonga and Samoa will be given Tier 1 status thanks to their on-field performances; the RLWC 2030 will take place across the Pacific and USA; it will have a 'Magic Round' format that will see the tournament descend on a new host city each week
articles.body:
The competitions will be played with a 'Magic Round' format that will see the teams arrive in a host city for a round of the tournaments before moving on.

The IRL board has also approved changes to international eligibility rules to increase the pool of players available to nations and they have endorsed the elevation of Tonga and Samoa to Men's Tier 1 status, subject to consultation with both teams.

The elevation of Samoa and Tonga as Tier 1 nations would be in recognition of their performances on and off the field, with both nations reaching the semi-finals of RLWC26. Samoa became the first Pacific nation to play in a World Cup final in 2022, while Tonga are the only Tier 2 nation to have defeated Australia, England and New Zealand.

The IRL board has also agreed to extend the eligibility criteria for players to be eligible to represent their nation of heritage if either they, a parent, a grandparent or a great grandparent were born there, the great grandparent element being added.

The decision comes off the back of a submission from Cook Islands given their small population of less than 20,000 and the movement of Cook Islanders to larger countries for work, study or other purposes.

The wheelchair tournament looks set to be hosted in France at the same time, while the men's tournament will increase from 10 to 12 teams, with the women's increasing from eight to 10.

IRL chair Troy Grant said: "The IRL board has decided that the next Rugby League World Cup for men and women in 2030 will be staged in the Pacific-USA. The next Wheelchair World Cup is going to be run at the same time in France.

"This is a strategy to maximise the interest of broadcasters, government partners and fans in the current World Cup, which has regularly broken records for crowds and the number of television viewers because of the outstanding skill, intensity and passion of the players and teams.

"At the same time we want to take advantage of opportunities that are opening up in new frontiers where the Rugby League World Cup hasn't previously been played.

"The World Cup under its current format runs for five weeks and RLWC30 is going to be run in five locations across the Pacific and USA. We haven't decided where yet; we are going to market and will look at the strategic placement of which cities we go to.

"The cities will be ones that have the appropriate stadia to run matches over multiple days to get all of the pool matches played in one location.

"This will be similar to a Magic Round, so IRL Rugby League World Cup 2030 will arrive in town, the stadium will be activated and there will be a lot of opportunities to promote the teams and the game. The World Cup will then move to the next city that is identified.

"There are three weeks where every nation is involved and then we have semi-finals and finals.

"The format for what that will look like is yet to be decided and nations were asked for feedback during the IRL AGM and Congress in Sydney over the weekend."

The IRL board has also proposed that the 2034 Rugby League World Cup be played under a similar format in Europe, coinciding with the 100th anniversary of the game in France, which was behind the establishment of the World Cup in 1954.

articles.title: Ireland rugby: Sean Jansen ruled out of Fiji and South Africa games with knee injury
articles.summary: Sean Jansen is ruled out of the remainder of Ireland's Nations Championship campaign with a knee injury, further depleting head coach Andy Farrell's options at number eight.
articles.body:
Sean Jansen has been ruled out of the remainder of Ireland's Nations Championship campaign with a knee injury, further depleting head coach Andy Farrell's options at number eight.

With Caelan Doris and Jack Conan already injured, Jansen was forced off during Friday's 42-12 win over Argentina in Dublin and will return to Connacht to continue his rehabilitation.

Hooker Dan Sheehan will miss Saturday's home match with Fiji (20:10 GMT) after sustaining a concussion against the Pumas, but the coaching staff are "hopeful" wing Rob Baloucoune (cramp) and flanker Josh van der Flier (ankle) will be available.

Sheehan - squad captain in Doris' absence - is a doubt for the South Africa game on 21 November as he undergoes 12-day return-to-play protocols.

With mounting back-row injury issues, uncapped Ulster forward David McCann has been called up, while Gus McCarthy has joined the squad to boost Farrell's options at hooker.

Centre Bundee Aki, a late withdrawal from the Argentina game with illness, is expected to resume full training on Tuesday.

After facing Fiji and back-to-back world champions South Africa at Aviva Stadium, Ireland will travel to Twickenham for a finals weekend fixture.

McCann and McCarthy were originally named in the Ireland XV squad for their fixture against Fiji 'A' in Cork on 20 November.

Tom Ahern (neck), Ethan McIlroy (thumb) and Michael Milne (ankle) have all been ruled out of the XV game, with Fineen Wycherley, Todd Lawlor and Jeremy Loughman called up.

articles.title: Nations Championship: England's Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Tom Curry ruled out of rest of tournament
articles.summary: Steve Borthwick's side have been hit by a raft of injuries ahead of their Nations Championship clash against Japan; Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Tom Curry have been ruled out of the autumn series
articles.body:
It comes as Steve Borthwick's side has been hit with a series of injuries ahead of their clash against Japan on Saturday.

Seb Atkinson, who came off in the second-half of England's 45-22 win against Australia, is set to miss the match with a hip injury, along with Ollie Chessum (shoulder) and George Furbank (groin).

England are optimistic the trio will be available for their clash against New Zealand at Allianz Stadium on Saturday, November 21.

Feyi-Waboso sustained an injury to his right ankle during the first-half of England's clash against the Wallabies, following a hip-drop tackle by Australia prop Angus Bell.

Bell was later sent to the sin bin, with Henry Pollock coming on to replace Feyi-Waboso on the wing at half-time. Pollock would go on to score twice.

The Exeter winger's absence could see Borthwick call on Saracens fliers Noah Caluori or Tobias Elliott for England's clash against Japan.

It would be Caluori's third cap for England, having made his senior debut during their Nations Championship clash against Fiji in July.

Centres Joe Marchant and Will Joseph could also be considered as wing options, while Fraser Dingwall or Max Ojomoh are likely to take the No 12 jersey in place of Atkinson.

Curry did not feature in England's win over Australia after he sustained a hip injury during training last week.

Borthwick revealed after Sunday's win that his brother, Ben Curry, was unlikely to start against Japan, despite the openside enjoying an excellent outing against the Wallabies.

It is likely Borthwick could deploy Freddie Steward at full-back in place of Furbank and keep Marcus Smith on the bench as utility cover.

England's 36-player squad returned to Pennyhill Park on Monday to prepare for this weekend's clash, with Jack Kenningham and Max Hicks both being drafted into the squad as back-row cover for Ben Curry and Chessum.

Meanwhile, Archie McParland has returned to the training squad after recovering from a calf injury.

Rehabilitation: Seb Atkinson (Gloucester Rugby), Ollie Chessum (Leicester Tigers), George Furbank (Harlequins)

articles.title: Immanuel Feyi-Waboso: England wing out of Nation Championship with ankle injury
articles.summary: England wing Immanuel Feyi-Waboso is ruled out of the rest of the Nations Championship as his injury misfortune continues.
articles.body:
England wing Immanuel Feyi-Waboso has been ruled out of the rest of the Nations Championship as his injury misfortune continues.

The 23-year-old injured his ankle in the first half of Sunday's 45-22 win over Australia in a "hip-drop" tackle by Angus Bell, for which the Wallabies prop received a yellow card.

England will also be without a handful of other key players for the match against Japan on Saturday, with Seb Atkinson, forward Ollie Chessum and full-back George Furbank all ruled out.

In a further blow, it has been confirmed experienced flanker Tom Curry will not feature this autumn after feeling discomfort in his hip.

Newcastle's uncapped flanker Max Hicks has been called into the 36-man squad, along with Harlequins' Jack Kenningham, while scrum-half Archie McParland, centre Max Ojomoh and wings Noah Calouri and Tobias Elliott are also included.

After hosting the Brave Blossoms in Twickenham, England face the in-form New Zealand All Blacks at Allianz Stadium on Saturday, 21 November.

The finals weekend takes place between 27-29 November.

England make massive step up in Australia victory

England swat aside Wallabies to back up Borthwick

Injuries take gloss off dominant display

Monday's injury update has taken the gloss off an exceptional England display against Australia, as Steve Borthwick's side produced their best performance of the year in a seven-try humbling of the Wallabies.

After bursting on to the international scene at the start of 2024, Feyi-Waboso has established himself as an X-factor talent but has been beset by injuries.

He missed the Six Nations in 2025 after undergoing shoulder surgery and was absent from this year's edition with a hamstring injury.

Feyi-Waboso was one of England's best players in the July leg of the Nations Championship, and had recovered from a hamstring problem picked up on club duty to start against Australia in a potent back three with Furbank and Tommy Freeman.

But Feyi-Waboso suffered his latest injury in the 32nd minute after the tackle by Bell and was replaced on the wing by Henry Pollock, normally a back row, after half-time.

Meanwhile, with Atkinson absent with a hip problem, Borthwick will need to field a new centre combination, meaning Fraser Dingwall or Max Ojomoh are in line to play at inside-centre.

At full-back, Furbank produced a consummate performance in his first England game in two years, but now will miss at least the Japan match because of a groin niggle.

It is hoped Atkinson and Furbank - as well as vice-captain Chessum, who has a shoulder injury - will all be available to face the All Blacks in 12 days' time.

articles.title: Wales v New Zealand: Aaron Wainwright injury doubt for Nations Championship match
articles.summary: Number eight Aaron Wainwright is a major Wales concern for the Nations Championship game against New Zealand on Saturday in Cardiff.
articles.body:
Number eight Aaron Wainwright has emerged as a major injury concern for Wales' Nations Championship game against New Zealand in Cardiff on Saturday.

The 29-year-old picked up a leg injury and has since been seen in a protective boot. He did not train on Tuesday.

Head coach Steve Tandy will name his team on Thursday and the absence of the former Dragons player would be a major blow.

Wainwright started in the 28-21 victory against Japan last Saturday and was the most experienced forward in the squad.

The Leicester number eight, who was winning his 71st cap, is also Wales' most effective forward ball-carrier.

New Zealand wing Will Jordan will miss the game because of a hamstring injury but centre Jordie Barrett is available for selection to face Wales after passing his head injury assessment (HIA) protocols.

Smiling Rees-Zammit has no fear of All Blacks

Wales should make fly-half change - Shanklin

Recalled Taine Basham would be the leading contender to replace Wainwright on Saturday, with Scarlets back-rower Taine Plumtree providing the other option in the squad.

Basham was rewarded with a squad call-up having been the form number eight in Welsh domestic rugby this season.

The Cardiff number eight has not played for Wales since the 2024 Six Nations, while his previous start to that was in 2022.

After the All Blacks match, Wales will host Australia on 21 November, before the Nations Championship finals weekend at the end of the month, hosted by the Allianz Stadium at Twickenham.

Wales currently lie fifth out of sixth in the northern hemisphere table after two wins from four matches.

Listen live on BBC Radio Wales, BBC Radio Cymru and BBC Radio 5Live

Trying to find the next Aaron Wainwright

Wales assistant coach Dan Lydiate says Wainwright has not been completely ruled out yet but accepts he could miss the weekend's action.

"He picked up a bit of a knock, it's a minor injury and he's walking around in a boot at the minute, but it's more precautionary," said Lydiate.

"We've been lucky enough with Wainwright that he's been quite robust over the years. The medical staff are working as quick as they can to turn him around.

"I don't know if he'll be available this week, but they're doing everything in their power to make sure he is."

Lydiate recognised the significance of Wainwright's potential absence but backs the squad's depth.

"He's such a leader in terms of his ball-carrying ability and a quality player like Aaron is a potential loss because you want your best players on the field," said Lydiate

"If that is the case, it will give someone else an opportunity, and you never know, we might find the next Aaron Wainwright."

articles.title: Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup: Spectacular England still short of best form
articles.summary: England are into the Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup final after thrashing Australia 86-18 - but still have not hit peak form, according to try-scorer Rob Hawkins.
articles.body:
Rob Hawkins laughed when asked by BBC Sport whether he had been practising his dives.

The question was prompted by some spectacular athleticism as he scored five tries to help England crush Australia 86-18 in Tuesday's Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup semi-final in Wollongong, Australia.

"It's just off-the-cuff stuff when needed," he said. "Some of the kicks were cautious!"

The man who had provided many of those kicks, Nathan Collins, was sitting beside him. He did not disagree.

"He makes my bad kicks look good!" Collins said. "It is great to have him there to sweep up. He's great to play with and against."

England have reason to be in good spirits as they prepare for a fifth successive World Cup final, the fourth in a row against great rivals France.

They are looking to defend the title they won on home ground four years ago, a narrow 28-24 victory in Manchester .

All of the three previous finals between the two teams have been tight: France won 42-40 in Gillingham in 2013, and 38-34 in Perpignan in 2017.

England seemed to set themselves up perfectly for Friday's final, scoring 15 tries against Australia. Hawkins' five scores, plus five conversions, took his personal points tally to 30 points.

His best try, and the standout from the whole game, was the third one - a long-range punt from England seemed to be a shot to nothing, but not where Hawkins was concerned.

He chased it down and, millimetres away from the dead-ball line, managed to grab the ball and get it down under huge pressure from Adam Tannock, who he had outpaced.

Yet Hawkins thought his and England's performances were far from perfect.

"Wouldn't say we are 10 out of 10 yet, there are still good a good few things to look at," he said. "Today was a six or seven. Hopefully the best is to come on Friday.

"Today was satisfying but not easy. We had the crowd to fight and a ruthless Australian team. But we are happy with the result."

England will now reset for their latest showdown with France, which will kick off at 08:45 GMT on Friday at WIN Entertainment Centre.

England thrash Australia to reach Wheelchair RL World Cup final

How Hawkins overcame illness to star for England

Chair skills, quick brain - how O'Neill adapted to wheelchair rugby league

Collins said England will need to repeat their dominant performance against Australia, and more, to beat the only other nation ever to win the world title.

"We've got to do what we did today, stick to the process Tom [Coyd, the England coach] has put in front of us," he said. "It looks like a good game, but there is still plenty to do.

"We are used to big games, league titles and Challenge Cups. This is a step up from that, so we go again."

Like many of the squad, Collins has had to overcome huge off-field challenges to get in a position to face the major challenges on the pitch.

Born with dwarfism, he played running rugby league as a child before being told he was too small. So, Collins moved into the wheelchair sport and made his England debut aged 16.

Now 26, he is a veteran of the team preparing for his third World Cup final, having won one, lost one.

"It has given me a lease of life," Collins said of his life in rugby league. "I have met so many amazing people along the way.

"At 16 I was straight in at the deep end, I couldn't think about it, just had to do it. Not many people get those chances at 16. I have grown with the game, I feel like I have gone on the level up with it.

"I'm proud of what we have achieved, on and off the pitch. It would mean a lot to bring that trophy home again.

"Looking in the corner of the stadium and seeing the wall of white [shirted England fans], it was amazing, hopefully we will see that again on Friday."

England will hope it is only the French players they have to deal with in the final, after bizarre scenes involving an official in 2022.

French referee Laurent Abrial, who officiated the 2022 World Cup final, was suspended until January this year after he "brought the game into disrepute through unacceptable behaviour".

An International Rugby League misconduct committee found Abrial made "obscene gestures that could have incited the crowd".

Abrial was the defence referee during the final and in the closing stages protested by gesticulating wildly after having a decision overruled by attack referee Ollie Cruickshank.

"The referees will make a decision on the day, we are just there to play the game," said Hawkins. "Our win overshadowed the decisions made. The officiating at this World Cup has been superb."

articles.title: England focused on ensuring Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Tom Curry get fit for Rugby World Cup
articles.summary: Immanuel Feyi-Waboso and Tom Curry have been laid low by injury and England are now focused on ensuring they will be fit for next year's Rugby World Cup; Kevin Sinfield also addressed the report that came out that said there was a squad rift in England
articles.body:
Feyi-Waboso will miss the rest of the autumn because of an ankle injury sustained in Sunday's 44-22 mauling of Australia, robbing England of their most dangerous attacking threat.

British and Irish Lions flanker Curry will sit out all four Nations Championship matches at Allianz Stadium this month after aggravating a long-standing hip condition in training last week.

Both players will travel to next year's World Cup in Australia if fit, but have concerning injury records that paint an uncertain picture over their involvement.

Under the current agreement between England and the Prem clubs, head coach Steve Borthwick now has greater control over the 25 members of his elite player squad, including final say on workload and medical matters.

"The best high-performance environments have the right amount of care and the right amount of challenge," assistant coach Sir Kevin Sinfield said.

"How Tom's managed, looked after and supported over this next period of time will be really important for him.

"He's still a young man and we're a better squad when he's around. He's a world-class player.

"The agreement that's in place hopefully will ensure brilliant collaboration between club and country so that Tom plays for a long, long time, and he can be at his very best when he's in and out of camp.

"Manny's had a run of injuries now and hopefully that can be the last one for some time. I think it's because of the nature of how he's put together - he's that powerful.

"What you tend to find is players either get a load of injuries at the start of their careers or get them towards the back end.

"Hopefully we can get him fully fit for a long period of time and Exeter get to see the best of him too. Again the collaboration is going to be really important for us."

Feyi-Waboso's unique ability to beat defenders was on full display at Twickenham against the Wallabies on Sunday and Sinfield described his performance as "world class", adding "he's our Jason Robinson" in reference to the cross-code great.

His absence creates a vacancy on the wing for Saturday's Test against Japan and whoever is selected will be instructed to play to their own strengths.

"There aren't many Mannys kicking around, so to go like-for-like is difficult," Sinfield said.

"We can't ask somebody to come in and play like Manny, but we can ask them to come in and bring the best of themselves."

Gloucester's in-form outside back Will Joseph is one of the players looking to fill his boots and Sinfield insists the younger brother of former England and British and Irish Lion Jonathan, is ready to take his chance if selected.

"What a player he is," Sinfield said. "He beats people. He's got great balance. He's a good defender with unbelievable power and speed off the mark.

"He's a special player. Some of the bits he's done in training have been 'wow' moments. He can play."

Sinfield: Don't give the report too much credit for performance

Sinfield also addressed England's strong performance against Australia following a report which garnered a lot of attention.

The Times reported some England players lost faith in Borthwick during a summer campaign which included a 45-21 defeat to world champions South Africa and a nervy win over Argentina.

It is alleged players objected to Borthwick's treatment of them, that he was involved in a training ground bust-up with Ellis Genge and that they wanted RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney - who this week unequivocally backed the head coach - to listen to their gripes.

Both Borthwick and captain Maro Itoje rejected the claims following the win over Australia, Jamie George said England's players were "hurt" by the report , and Sinfield agrees that England were "committed" and kept out the "outside noise".

However, he is wary to give the report too much credit when it comes to how England played.

"The performance was important," Sinfield said.

"I thought the lads showed how committed and determined they were and showed how together they are.

"There was some outside noise at the back end of the week. I thought Steve handled it really well. It was really nice to see a full Twickenham on Sunday afternoon, who were pretty happy come the 80th minute.

"I have been impressed by our senior players all the way through.

"I've been here four years now. I think the credibility we give that article and the noise, if we're suggesting that the performance was just down to that, it's unfair on the lads. It's unfair on everybody who's involved with this team.

"There's been a lot of work over a period of time of pushing our performances and trying to get better and better. I thought they did a great job of that on weekend. The challenge for us is to do it again this week, to try and come out."

articles.title: Immanuel Feyi-Waboso is our Jason Robinson - Kevin Sinfield
articles.summary: Immanuel Feyi-Waboso is the 2026 team's equivalent of Rugby World Cup winner Jason Robinson says assistant coach Kevin Sinfield.
articles.body:
Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, England's prolific but injury-prone wing, is the 2026 team's equivalent of Rugby World Cup winner Jason Robinson says assistant coach Kevin Sinfield.

Feyi-Waboso has scored nine tries in 17 appearances for England since making his Test debut against Italy in 2024.

However, his progress with England has been checked by a string of injuries.

He missed the 2025 Six Nations with a shoulder injury, while his 2026 tournament was ended by a hamstring injury sustained in training before England's opening-round win over Wales.

He returned this summer, scoring in wins over Fiji and Argentina, but suffered an autumn-ending ankle injury in the first half of Sunday's match against Australia.

Robinson, whose acceleration and side-step brought him 28 tries in 51 appearances for England between 2001 and 2007, tore his hamstring in the Rugby World Cup final defeat by South Africa in his final Test.

"He is our Jason Robinson," said Sinfield, who played against Robinson during the pair's days in rugby league.

"When you have a player who is that explosive and that powerful sometimes a run of injuries just happens.

"He's across everything to do with his body and hopefully we get him back firing as soon as we can.

"That collaboration [between England and Feyi-Waboso's club Exeter] is going be really important because these guys play a lot of rugby.

"Making sure they're fit for those big games is going to be really important."

England have the final say over the fitness and conditioning of centrally-contracted players such as Feyi-Waboso, but there have been disagreements in the past with Exeter over his treatment.

Relations have since improved with England signing off Fey-Waboso's return for June's Prem final, only three weeks after he suffered a facial fracture.

Feyi-Waboso played on after suffering his ankle injury in the 32nd minute of Sunday's 45-22 win over the Wallabies, hobbling his way to half-time before being replaced.

Sinfield said that the desire of Feyi-Waboso, who is studying medicine, to stay on the pitch swayed the decision to keep him on.

"It's getting the balance right, because the player is telling you he wants to try and run it off," said Sinfield.

"You can't scan anyone on the grass, so you're looking at it with your eyes. I think it's only right for us, as coaches, that we listen to players."

England will be without Ollie Chessum, George Furbank and Seb Atkinson for Saturday's match against Japan, while flanker Tom Curry has, like Feyi-Waboso, been ruled out of the entire autumn campaign after he aggravated a long-standing hip issue.

Saracens' 20-year-old Noah Caluori, who made a try-scoring England debut against Fiji in July, has been called up in Feyi-Waboso's place.

Live on BBC Radio 5 Live, the BBC Sport website and app

£13m and counting - Sinfield focused on latest MND drive

Sinfield was knighted last month for his services to both codes of rugby and for raising money and awareness about motor neurone disease.

Sinfield's friend and former Leeds Rhinos team-mate Rob Burrow died from MND in June 2024 at the age of 41.

Sinfield has raised more than £13m for charities involved in attempting to support those with the disease and find a cure, running seven ultra marathons in seven days last month in his most recent challenge.

He now plans to run seven marathons in seven days in New Zealand and Australia in late May to help global collaboration in research. NRL star Jai Arrow and former Wallaby Nathan Charles have recently been diagnosed, raising the profile of MND in Australia.

"It's been a great journey and it's important we continue because there's no cure," said Sinfield. "We've got to carry on."

articles.title: Tomas Francis: Wales prop targets fourth World Cup after international return
articles.summary: Wales prop Tomas Francis says the prospect of playing in a fourth World Cup drives him on.
articles.body:
Wales prop Tomas Francis says the prospect of playing in a fourth World Cup drives him on.

Francis, 34, could become part of an exclusive Welsh group next year if he is named for a fourth global tournament in Australia.

Only Gareth Thomas, Stephen Jones, Gethin Jenkins, Alun Wyn Jones and George North have achieved that accolade for Wales.

Francis says he would have laughed if somebody had told him during his first World Cup in 2015 that 12 years later he might complete a quartet of competitions.

"You never think far ahead and I was happy to get one cap then," said Francis.

"You just keep trying to improve and stay in that competition for the jersey.

"So now a [fourth World Cup], is a great carrot to have."

Recalled Francis relishing chance to help Wales

Wainwright gives Wales injury scare for All Blacks

Smiling Rees-Zammit has no fear of All Blacks

Following the 2023 World Cup, Francis took a break from international rugby after leaving Ospreys to join French Pro D2 side Provence.

"I think for about two-and-a half years I was away for eight nights and I had two young girls," said Francis.

"As a father you can't get that time back. I'd given my all for two World Cup cycles, so for Welsh rugby and me, it was right to have a little time away.

"It gave time [for Wales] to find other options and give others games."

Francis never closed the door on returning.

"I told Gats [former Wales head coach Warren Gatland] if you need me I am around and he passed that onto Steve [Tandy]," said Francis.

"You always want that chance to put that jersey on and it's been amazing to get back out there."

And Francis says still gets the pre-match butterflies.

"I still want to run away on game day and not go and play and those are the nerves that drive me," said Francis.

"I live on those nerves on game day. The day I lose that, I'll know it's time not to be here."

Wales should make fly-half change - Shanklin

Why Wales have a lot to prove despite beating Japan

Wales let themselves down despite win - Lake

Francis was not part of the Wales squad that lost a record 18 Tests in a row or suffered 21 losses in 23 internationals between October 2023 and February 2026.

Wales never really replaced him and he returned for this year's Six Nations after a Test break of 26 months.

He was a replacement in the opening defeats against England in February with Archie Griffin starting, before Francis was handed the number three shirt for the next four matches, including the final win against Italy.

Francis was given the summer off by Wales as he moved from France to Manchester where he linked up with English side Sale.

"The rugby's been good, there's some world-class players there," said Francis.

"The environment's a bit different to the second division in France in that respect, but I've enjoyed it.

"The results haven't gone for us yet, but it's a new team.

"There are exciting youngsters there and they've also brought in some old heads. Hopefully we can kick on when we click."

Listen live on BBC Radio Wales, BBC Radio Cymru and BBC Radio 5Live

Francis returned to Wales for this November campaign after being named in the squad alongside fellow tight-head props Griffin and Dillon Lewis, who started the first three Nations Championship matches in July.

With Griffin starting the 28-21 win against Japan in Cardiff last weekend, Francis, who is the oldest member of the squad, came off the replacements bench to win his 83rd cap.

Wales emulated their victory against Japan in Cardiff in November 2025 but Francis states the post-match reaction was different.

"In the changing room afterwards, we weren't celebrating like the last time we beat Japan," said Francis.

"It was quite sombre because we knew we hadn't hit the heights we wanted to.

"We'd left points out there and hadn't put in the performance we wanted so we're now not celebrating just scraping a win.

"We're looking at what's next and asking how we get better."

The New Zealand challenge is next as Wales look to break a 34-match losing sequence against the All Blacks that stretches back to 1953.

Francis says it is these sort of event that attracted him back to the international stage.

"It was an amazing occasion," said Francis.

"I remember watching Wales play New Zealand in Cardiff last year when I was in France. I sat at home and got goosebumps."

With concerns about the size of the Cardiff crowd, Francis hopes Wales can inspire and be inspired by the home faithful.

"We talk about the Principality Stadium as a group, that we want to try and get the crowd in the game as much as possible," said Francis.

"For me, it might be a scrum or a maul penalty or it could be Zammo [Louis Rees-Zammit] or Blair [Murray] going through tackles.

"You hear the electricity in that stadium and it lifts us. The more moments we can develop like that, the more fans we can get to watch and the more we keep pushing each other.

"It's the best ground in the world with the roof closed and when the supporters are behind you, it's amazing."

Fixtures and standings as Nations Championship returns

Francis is approaching the twilight of an international career that has spanned more than a decade.

He was part of a Wales side that won a Grand Slam, two Six Nations titles and reached number one in the world in 2019 following a record 14-match winning sequence.

Wales have been in decline since those heady days but Francis hopes the glory years will return for the current crop.

"This is an exciting time and I believe the ceiling is massive for this group," said Francis.

"I can confidently say I'm not going to be here when they reach their full potential because of my age, but I hope I can add to that journey.

"There were glory times in 2019 which we probably took a bit for granted when we were there.

"But there is no reason we can't come back."

articles.title: Steve McNamara v Nathan Cayless: Who has hardest job on Humberside?
articles.summary: A look ahead to Hull FC and Hull KR's respective upcoming seasons under new head coaches following disappointing Super League campaigns.
articles.body:
While the city's football club have acclimatised well to life back in the Premier League, British adventurer Karl Bushby has returned to his home city following a 28-year expedition around the world.

And it is all change for both of the city's rugby league clubs who are set to embark on new eras under fresh management.

Steve McNamara returns to take charge of Hull FC, 30 years after he left the club as a player, following a turbulent 2026 for the Black and Whites which led to the departure of the popular John Cartwright.

Over on the east side of the city, Nathan Cayless has been cherry-picked by the Robins as Super League-winner Willie Peters' successor for a Hull KR side looking to breathe new life into their credentials as title-winners.

So, who looks like they will have the hardest job on Humberside for the 2027 season?

Now just feels the right time - McNamara

Hull FC announced the appointment of McNamara in April while the 55-year-old was still an assistant coach at Warrington under the leadership of Sam Burgess.

The Black and Whites finished a disappointing 11th last term, the sixth consecutive year in which they have missed out on the play-offs, and McNamara knows the magnitude of the job he has on his hands to turn fortunes around.

In the off-season, Hull have already confirmed the signings of 10 new players, including Bailey Hodgson from Leigh, Arlix Da Costa from Catalans and six-time State of Origin series winner Daly Cherry-Evans.

Despite being away for 30 years following his move to Bradford Bulls as a player in 1996 - McNamara still has recent family ties to the club as son Ben, now of Castleford, plied his trade for Hull FC between 2020 and 2023.

"I'm really proud and honoured," McNamara told BBC Radio Humberside. "The history that it's got, and the great coaches that it's had, it's my time now to take over the baton.

"I've had opportunities in the past to come back but it's never been the right time – either for myself or the club. Now, it just feels right.

"I wouldn't have come back to the club now unless I felt it had a real opportunity for some growth and it had potential.

"We've got a big gap from where the other teams are quite clearly. The league position doesn't lie but I think this [team] has got more potential than any other team right now in Super League."

Hull FC sign Kerr and release forward Bell

Hull won just eight Super League games last season. They have only recorded fewer wins in a single campaign once (2024, with just three) this century.

Unlike his new squad, McNamara can remember a time when Hull FC were competing at the top of the game. He was in attendance as a young fan when the Black and Whites last won the top division over 43 years ago.

"In 1979, I was an eight-year-old with my dad and that was the first season I started watching them," he said.

"And then following them through the 1980s and '90s – and getting to captain the club. There's something deep down there.

"All we ask of the players now is they're all in, every single day.

"Anything that's happened in the past is irrelevant to most of us now. We have no baggage from that, we're coming in fresh. It's refreshing for everyone involved."

Settling into the Hull FC hotseat, the former Bradford Bulls boss can immediately put his own stamp on the side having also coached in France with Catalans, as well as in New Zealand and Australia.

There were complaints last season that Hull were not as fit as they should have been, and McNamara has taken steps to get the players in better shape.

On multiple occasions last season, including in two Hull derbies in July, the Black and Whites started strongly in the first half and blew out in the second.

He has brought in Nathan Mills from St Helens as the new medical high-performance specialist, as well as Jimmy McDaniel as head of performance from neighbouring Kingston Rovers, both labelled "world class" by McNamara.

"No disrespect to anyone else but I don't think the investment in that area [strength and conditioning] has been good enough and we've backed some high-quality people to be involved in our organisation," McNamara said.

In paying Warrington a "substantial transfer fee to secure McNamara's services", , external the implication is the Hull board will give McNamara time to implement big, and necessary, changes.

"It's a juggernaut of a club," McNamara added. "The one consistent thing it has had over recent years is the amount of supporters that go, home and away.

"We'll finish where we deserve to finish. How we conduct ourselves, on and off the field, between now and the end of the season.

"If we keep improving, you don't know when you're going to stop improving."

It is a different sort of new start for Nathan Cayless at Hull KR.

Unlike McNamara, this is the 48-year-old's first job as a head coach, and unlike McNamara, the Robins are aiming to focus on evolution next year, rather than revolution.

The blueprint should not be ripped up following Hull KR's stunning 2025 season in which they completed a historic treble before wrapping up all four major honours by winning the World Club Challenge in February.

But a disappointing defence of their Super League crown last season means a change in management could still help freshen things up for a squad which largely remains from two campaigns ago.

While McNamara is Hull through and through, Cayless has spent his entire club career in the NRL, having spent 13 years as a player for the Parramatta Eels before becoming an assistant coach for the Sydney-based club following his retirement in 2010.

"A lot of preparation work has already been done," Cayless told BBC Radio Humberside.

"I've really been getting itchy feet. It [seeing Craven Park for the first time] was surreal. I didn't get the opportunity to play over here but now to be a part of it is very exciting.

"I can't thank everyone enough for making us all feel welcome, my wife and I.

"I love how closely the community is tied into the team.

"I've got a load of really good mates that have either worked or played here, who have said nothing but great things - not only the club, but the people of the area, the community.

"It reminds me of Parramatta. It's a real club feel and I've felt that for the entire period I've been here so far."

'We get one crack at life, make sure you have no regrets'

First in Cayless' in-tray will be finding the key to unlock the best form of influential half-back Mikey Lewis.

On too many occasions last season, it was a case of if you could stop Lewis, you could stop the Robins entirely.

Cayless will need to tap into Lewis, as well as finding more creativity on a consistent basis from the other backs at his disposal if former Man of Steel Lewis is misfiring.

Despite the focus on evolving the current playing staff, the Hull KR board do not want a 'Willie Peters mark two' type of coach, even if the Australian guided the club to their first league championship in 40 years.

Cayless is open on having held conversations with Peters over recent months.

The former New Zealand international says Peters was clear on how much "care and love" is put into the club by the staff, highlighting the support he felt from the board was one of the key reasons in taking the job.

"When this opportunity arose, we sat down as a family and without our kids' buy-in it was going to be pretty difficult to do," Cayless told BBC Radio Humberside.

"We get one crack at life, and you want to make sure you have no regrets.

"I've been coaching for 12 years now and deliberately taking my time."

There are some underlying similarities between the two coaches though despite the obvious differences.

Both McNamara and Cayless continuously stressed the importance of "improving" their respective sides as they come in new having been assistants last year.

So, as a slightly more unknown quantity to McNamara, what can Kingston Rovers fans expect from a Cayless side next year?

"What I will promise, we're going to work really hard throughout pre-season," Cayless said.

"I promise that the team is going to be ready to start pre-season. They'll [the players] make their community proud of how they perform.

"These guys that are in the stands, if they're proud of the performance of the team, the results will look after themselves."

With three months before the start of the Super League season, there is of course still lots of time for both teams to improve and hit the ground running immediately.

What does seem clear is these old foes have gone in different directions in order to achieve that sought-after improvement.

articles.title: Immanuel Feyi-Waboso: England winger's injury hopefully not serious
articles.summary: Exeter boss Rob Baxter hopes the ankle injury Immanuel Feyi-Waboso suffered while playing for England will not be too serious.
articles.body:
Exeter boss Rob Baxter hopes the ankle injury Immanuel Feyi-Waboso suffered while playing for England will not be too serious.

The 23-year-old was forced off at half-time of Sunday's 45-22 Nations Championship win over Australia at Twickenham.

It has ended his involvement with England over the rest of the autumn international period, but he could figure for Exeter again before the end of the year.

Feyi-Waboso will meet with a surgeon on Thursday to review scans on the injury before a detailed recovery plan is devised.

"The balance of opinion at the moment, both from ourselves and England, is that he's unlikely to require an operation," Baxter told BBC Sport.

"If it's a decent high ankle sprain, I think you're talking a minimum of four to six weeks really, but obviously it's just so difficult to know.

"Manny's the kind of guy, sometimes he might be running on this in a week's time and then that changes the whole timescale, so it's a little early to say yet."

England wing Feyi-Waboso out of Nations Championship

Exeter's Wyatt suffers fresh injury blow

Injured Exeter winger Ridl to miss most of season

It is the latest blow to Exeter's back three which has endured a host of injuries this season.

Campbell Ridl is out for most of the campaign with a knee ligament injury while Tommy Wyatt is a month away from fitness after an ankle problem.

Paul Brown-Bampoe returned to action in the Prem Rugby Cup loss to Bath last week having been out since heel surgery over the summer.

Exeter have been forced to play centre Zack Wimbush out wide in recent weeks, although Dallas McLeod has joined up with the club after his summer move from New Zealand to strengthen the area.

"That's kind of how it happens, you've just got to get on with things," added Baxter.

"We've just got to hope we get through this international period without any further injuries.

"We're obviously getting more guys up and running and getting good game time into them through his Prem Cup period.

"You've got to look on the positives of it, let's hope this injury to Manny isn't too bad and he can crack on in this period.

"Hopefully, Paul (Brown-Bampoe) will get right up to speed. If we can get Manny back in that four to six week period - who knows, it might be longer - hopefully we can start to pull things together a bit there."

articles.title: Super League approves expansion to 15 teams for 2027 season
articles.summary: Super League says its shareholders have agreed to expand the league from 14 clubs to 15 for the 2027 season.
articles.body:
Super League has said its shareholders have agreed to expand the league from 14 clubs to 15 for the 2027 season.

The league expanded from 12 to 14 teams in time for 2026, allowing Bradford Bulls, York Knights and Toulouse Olympique to join, with Salford Red Devils dropping out after a financially tumultuous 2025 campaign.

It will be the first time the league has operated with 15 clubs, with the top flight running with 12 for much of its existence apart from spells with 14 teams in 2000, from 2009 to 2014 and last season.

"[Super League (Europe)] has passed their decision on to the Rugby Football League board," a league statement said. , external

"The RFL Board will now set out criteria and assemble a panel to run the process to judge against it.

"A recommendation will be made in due course."

Super League to expand to 14 teams from 2026

Wakefield top as all 14 Super League clubs stay for 2027

The expansion means that London Broncos could be in line to rejoin Super League, having won the Championship Grand Final and 1895 Cup last season.

The Broncos came in 16th on the yearly grading list, below fellow Championship side Barrow Raiders, despite a season in which they set the pace in the second tier.

The club - which now has the backing of Australian businessman Grant Wechsel and former Brisbane Broncos star Darren Lockyer - was overlooked 12 months ago when Bradford, York and Toulouse joined the expanded 14-team competition for 2026.

Super League is yet to agree a new title sponsorship deal, finalise broadcast negotiations or even its fixtures for the 2027 campaign.

It is understood any completed investment deal with Australian governing body the National Rugby League (NRL) would insist on Broncos featuring in the top flight.

London ready to take leap with expansion - analysis

BBC Rugby League commentator Matt Newsum

It appears the final hurdles to the London Broncos' inclusion in the 2027 Super League competition are finally being overcome after the member clubs agreed to the expansion to 15 clubs.

The Broncos are ready to make the leap, backed by the finance of Australian mining businessman Wechsel and former Australia star Lockyer, after a season of dominance in the second tier.

They actually graded lower than Championship rivals Barrow under the system created by the game's strategic partner IMG, because the data is taken from a three-year cycle and the season post former owner David Hughes' investment in the club has to be taken into account.

Yet the forecast financially would put London well ahead of their peers as borne out by their recruitment, and their ability to weather a lack of central funding as part of their conditions in joining the top flight.

The NRL and its chairman Peter V'landys have maintained London are a major part of their proposals, with an investment deal also hoped to be completed, albeit expected to be deferred until 2028.

London were far too good for the second division last season and, unlike some of their peers, are ready to make the transition immediately.

However, depending on how the RFL board criteria and panel is set up, there may be criticism for a grading system that sceptics might say carries little weight, given its scores can be cast aside should the situation require it.

articles.title: France v South Africa: Antoine Dupont at fly-half for Paris match
articles.summary: France will take on world champions South Africa on Friday with captain Antoine Dupont filling in at fly-half because of a raft of injuries.
articles.body:
France captain Antoine Dupont will fill in at fly-half for Friday's Nations Championship game against world champions South Africa in Paris.

Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang, who was born and raised in London but moved to France as a 19-year-old after struggling to get a professional contract in England, will win his fourth cap on the wing.

Grandidier-Nkanang focused on Sevens, winning Olympic gold alongside Dupont in 2024 before making a successful switch back to the 15-a-side game with Pau.

Dupont, a specialist scrum-half with only a handful of appearances at 10, has been forced into fly-half by the absence of Matthieu Jalibert, Romain Ntamack, Thomas Ramos and Antoine Hastoy.

It had been expected that Maxime Lucu, another scrum-half, would play at fly-half.

Lucu came off the bench to replace Ntamack, who suffered a shoulder injury 32 minutes into Saturday's 54-17 victory over Fiji.

Lucu has the more recent experience as a starting fly-half at club level, having played at 10 for Bordeaux-Begles against Gloucester last month.

However, France coach Fabian Galthie has opted for Dupont, who filled in at fly-half for Toulouse during an injury crisis in the 2023-24 season.

Galthie has selected hooker Julien Marchand and number eight Gregory Alldritt, who was left out of this year's Six Nations, to counter the Springboks' forward power.

"I don't even know if Dupont's team-mates know exactly what he's going to do next, so he's just really playing on instinct, which is tough to handle," South Africa coach Erasmus said this week.

He has made only one change to the side that thrashed Italy 66-7 on Saturday, with Wilco Louw replacing former Bath prop Thomas du Toit.

South Africa have won nine of their past 10 Tests against France, including a 14-man victory last autumn and a one-point quarter-final victory at the 2023 World Cup.

France: Attissogbe; Grandidier-Nkanang, Gourgues, Moefana, Bielle-Biarrey; Dupont, Lucu; Falatea, Marchand, Gros, Verhaeghe, Guillard, Cros, Woki, Alldritt.

Replacements: Mauvaka, Neti, Montagne, Ollivon, Staniforth, Capilla, Desperes, Gailleton.

South Africa: Willemse; Arendse, Kriel, de Allende, Hooker; Feinberg-Mngomezulu, van den Berg; Nche, Marx, Louw, de Jager, Nortje, PS du Toit, Kolisi, Wiese.

Replacements: Wessels, Steenekamp, T du Toit, Mostert, Hanekom, de Villiers, Reinach, Libbok.

articles.title: Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup: Tom and Joe Coyd looking to take England to successive World Cup titles as France await in final
articles.summary: England Wheelchair men face France in the Rugby League World Cup Final from Wollongong on Friday, with head coach Tom Coyd and brother Joe leading the charge to second successive title; England beat Australia 86-18 in semi-final
articles.body:
Already a World Cup winning coach, Tom has been in charge of England for six years, with younger brother and star winger Joe scoring 12 tries on the way to their last national team success at 2022's tournament.

The task of securing a second world title in a row - something only Friday's opponents, France, have managed - is already a tall task, but Tom has battled with what he feels is an even tougher challenge throughout the tournament.

"[Coaching my brother] is the hardest thing I've ever done from a work perspective," Tom said. "But it's also the most rewarding.

"There are times when you have to give him a bit of a telling off.

"It's taught me loads about how to be a good brother and loads about how to be a good coach - hopefully, Joe agrees. But yeah, it is an interesting dynamic.

"I think there's a reason it doesn't happen very often because it can be really difficult. But, you know, in our quirky ways, Joe and I find a way to make it function. And I think it elevates the connection in the team."

His brother, Joe, echoes this sentiment.

"I've been lucky enough to do this for a while and it's such a special occasion and privilege every time.

"But having my brother and my dad alongside me sort of just sort of nudges it on a bit further.

"I know I'm in a very lucky and privileged place to be able to do the things that we get to do alongside my family."

The brothers are not the only two family members involved in the England World Cup setup.

Martin Coyd OBE is the general manager of the Wheelchair side, and, according to his sons, isn't afraid of getting stuck in with preparation himself.

"He's in camp with us. He's been busy fulfilling his responsibilities as a RFL board member, but he's been doing that alongside, you know, getting oily and repairing wheelchair parts and getting his hands dirty.

"He's been in the thick of it and he wouldn't have it any other way. It's been a joy to have this experience with him and with Joe and with all of us.

"As someone who's been at the head of the team for over a decade, he sort of sets the standard and drives the culture. He does a good job for us."

Mouth-watering France contest awaits England

Despite Coyd's side recording a thrilling 28-24 victory against Les Blues in the last World Cup final, their opponents have won two of the last three matches between the two sides since, with France retaining the Fassolette-Kielty trophy with a thrilling 32-28 win in the latest edition of the rivalry in November 2024.

Two years on, Coyd knows his opponents will be ready for World Cup revenge.

"Yeah, absolutely. I do [think it'll be a game of fine margins]," Tom said.

"That's World Cup and Test match football, isn't it - and France have been, you know, one of the leaders of the game internationally since it began.

"It's knockout sport, isn't it? Anything can happen on the day. So it's hugely important that we kind of ride those waves of expectation and get our framing right. I think your reality is the story you tell yourselves.

"When you're a team and you spend so much time together, controlling that narrative as a collective is super important. "So when the guys push out on Friday, I don't expect that they'll feel the weight of expectation.

"I expect them to feel confident knowing that they've kind of earned the right to be a fancied team.

"But France have that right, too. They've also been a high performing international outfit in the last four years and have beaten us in the last four years.

"So that's what makes it such an exciting contest on Friday."

articles.title: England v Japan: Eddie Jones sets sights on chaos and upset
articles.summary: Eddie Jones says Japan are drawing inspiration from Italy as they chase their own landmark win over England on Saturday.
articles.body:
Head coach Eddie Jones says Japan are drawing inspiration from Italy, who beat England for the first time in March, as the Brave Blossoms attempt to heap pressure back on Steve Borthwick with their own landmark win on Saturday.

Jones was sacked by England in December 2022 after a miserable autumn which ended in a 27-13 Twickenham defeat by South Africa and jeers from the home fans.

The Australian, 66, hopes to cause similar unrest on his return to Allianz Stadium this weekend.

"We're massive underdogs," Jones told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"We've got to find a way to disrupt an England side that's looking at New Zealand next week [England play the All Blacks on 21 November] and sometimes may be a little bit distracted.

"Our opportunity is to get in there, cause some havoc, cause some chaos, put off their game, get the crowd booing. Then the sky starts to come in on Twickenham and you never know what can happen.

"We've seen it happen with Italy and other countries."

Japan have lost all six of their previous Test meetings with England, most recently going down 54-19 on their autumn visit two years ago.

However Italy, who won for the first time in 33 attempts earlier this year, and Fiji, who broke their duck with a 30-22 success in 2023, have both secured maiden victories over England during Borthwick's reign.

Jones believes England's players are uniquely susceptible to pressure, given a level of scrutiny which is unprecedented in the rest of the global game.

A run of five successive defeats earlier this year, combined with reports of a rift between players and coaches, raised the stakes for England before Sunday's meeting with Australia.

However, Borthwick's players, who had insisted that the squad remains united, delivered an impressive 45-22 victory to vindicate their coach.

"The noise does get to the team and it can be pretty loud in England," said Jones, for whom Borthwick worked as an assistant during a previous stint with Japan and then with England.

"You've got a lot of newspapers, a lot of media, probably more than any other country in the world. Sometimes that can weigh down on the players and it's the job of the leadership to get the players thinking straight.

"Steve's an outstanding coach and a very intelligent man, and a really good coach. So I've got the highest respect for him."

England back row Henry Pollock scored two tries after replacing the injured Immanuel Feyi-Waboso on the wing at half-time against Australia, and has been tipped to make only his second start for his country on Saturday.

Having also scored a hat-trick off the bench against Fiji in July, Pollock is averaging a try every 22 minutes in the Nations Championship.

However, Jones believes the 21-year-old's sky-high strike-rate is not the best measure of him as a player.

"I wouldn't look too much into it," he said of Pollock's two scores against Australia.

"Everyone was licking the ice cream on Sunday. They were on the front foot, everyone's lining up to run the ball, there's no pressure in the game.

"He's a fast back rower, he got the ball in space and he's a talented player, there's no doubt about it, but you couldn't read into it any more than that."

Fly-half Ryunosuke Ito was plucked from university rugby by Jones, and made his debut against Italy in July without having ever played a professional match.

Ito scored his own solo try against Australia in August, neatly stepping through the Wallabies defence. , external

However the 21-year-old fourth-year student, who has established himself as Jones' first-choice fly-half, is required by Meiji University for a collegiate competition, meaning he is missing the northern hemisphere leg of Japan's Nations Championship campaign.

Ito will join top-flight Tokyo side Suntory Sungoliath next season, who have former New Zealand captain Sam Cane and Ireland and British and Irish Lions wing James Lowe in their squad.

"That's the uniqueness of Japanese rugby," added Jones.

articles.title: Ireland rugby: 'It's what I want' - Joey Carbery outlines ambition to win Test number 10 jersey
articles.summary: In an interview with the Ireland Rugby Social, Joey Carbery outlines his international ambitions, recalls his Munster exit and speaks about incoming Leinster boss Noel McNamara.
articles.body:
Having spent the past two years outside of the Irish system, Joey Carbery makes no bones about his ambitions heading into a World Cup year.

"Play for Ireland, I'll just go out there and say it," the fly-half tells the Ireland Rugby Social .

"It's what I want. It was a big reason to come home, to give these next three or four years the best shot I can. I want to let my rugby do the talking and hopefully that's enough."

With just two starts under his belt since rejoining Leinster from Bordeaux-Begles, Carbery missed out on Andy Farrell's latest Ireland squad, instead being included in Mark Sexton's Ireland XV panel for next week's match against Fiji 'A' in Cork.

Coincidentally, Carbery's last Test cap came in Ireland's November 2022 victory over Fiji.

"It's a foot back in the door of the Irish system and the way they play," added the 31-year-old.

"It's a pretty young squad to be involved with, there's a few older lads in it as well but it's nice to be back in the Irish fold."

The Ireland Rugby Social with Joey Carbery

Carbery stars as Leinster hammer Connacht in URC

New Zealand-born Carbery was long viewed as Johnny Sexton's heir apparent, serving as the legendary out-half's understudy at Leinster and Ireland.

He made his Ireland debut in the famous Chicago win over the All Blacks in November 2016 and, in 2018, was Sexton's deputy during the Grand Slam campaign before helping Leinster secure a Pro14 and Champions Cup double.

The problem soon became clear, though. While Leinster senior coach Stuart Lancaster saw Carbery's future at full-back, Ireland boss Joe Schmidt told the player he wouldn't pick him if he wasn't playing at fly-half.

With that, he left Leinster for rivals Munster in the summer of 2018 in a bid to boost his Test career.

"Ulster and Munster were on the table. It came down to whether I wanted to play for Ireland or not," recalled Carbery.

"I was told that if I wasn't playing 10 I wasn't going to be picked because Stuart in Leinster played me at 15 more than 10 because he thought I was a better 15.

"Joe said 'no, I want you as a 10, if you don't play there I can't pick you'. The 2019 World Cup was just on the horizon, I went to Munster in 2018 so that was coming up, that's how it all came about."

It wasn't all smooth sailing in red, though. Having already missed a significant number of games through injury, the emergence of Jack Crowley - who made his Ireland debut in Carbery's last cap - pushed him closer to the exit door.

Left out of Ireland's Six Nations and World Cup squads in 2023, Noel McNamara - with whom he had crossed paths at Leinster - asked if he would be interested in joining Bordeaux, the chance to experience the Top 14 in France proved irresistible.

"Mentally, I was in a bit of a rut," reflected the former Blackrock College star, whose injury woes in France restricted him to just four starts last season.

"It was a pretty awful way to finish [with Munster] because you go from starting to being completely cut off and getting no feedback and no answers.

"I remember Faz [Andy Farrell] even ringing me to say, 'look, you're not going to be in the World Cup squad' and I was like, 'I didn't even expect a call from you' because I hadn't played for the last six weeks. I didn't even think I'd get a call."

In addition to re-establishing himself as a contender for Ireland's 10 jersey, Carbery hopes to help Leinster's push back to the European summit, with the province having failed to win the Champions Cup during his eight years away.

And while this season is Leo Cullen's last as Leinster head coach, Carbery is thrilled by the prospect of linking back up with McNamara, who was confirmed as Cullen's successor last week.

"The way he's built his CV up, it's crazy the similarities between him and Joe [Schmidt]. Both were schoolteachers, both went to France and both came back to Leinster head coach role.

"I worked with him at underage and worked with him at Bordeaux. For a foreigner to come into a French group like that with the egos we had and to be listened to, the way he conducted himself and talked to the players was incredible.

"I think he's the perfect man for the job, it's really exciting, for me anyway, to be working with him again.

"As a person, a top man and a really good coach. That's a big part of being the Leinster coach because the squad is so big and you have internationals that won't even get into the matchday 15 sometimes so you have to be able to deal with that and understand that."

articles.title: Max Llewellyn: Wales centre inspired by Sonny Bill Williams ahead of All Blacks
articles.summary: Max Llewellyn is relishing taking on New Zealand with Wales after growing up watching the All Blacks win two World Cups.
articles.body:
After growing up admiring Sonny Bill Williams in action for New Zealand, Wales centre Max Llewellyn hopes to give the All Blacks some offloading headaches.

Llewellyn is poised to line up at inside centre when Steve Tandy's side welcome New Zealand to Cardiff in the Nations Championship on Saturday (14:10 GMT).

The 6ft 6in Gloucester back grew up watching the double-World Cup winning All Blacks side that featured Dan Carter, Richie McCaw, Ma'a Nonu, Sam Whitelock and Kieran Read.

Yet it was the sizeable frame of dual-code icon Williams - with his ability to free his arms and keep the ball alive - that caught the eye of Llewellyn.

"He was probably someone that I really enjoyed watching when growing up," said the 27-year-old.

"I was a centre, he was a centre and he had a similar frame. I really enjoyed what he did in bringing the offload into rugby.

"That kind of changed the game a bit and was something that I looked at and wanted to emulate."

Wales prop Francis targets fourth World Cup

Wainwright gives Wales injury scare for All Blacks

Llewellyn has done something that not many Welsh rugby players have - he has beaten New Zealand.

That was in the 2019 World Rugby Under-20 Championship in Argentina, but few expect that shock age-grade success to be repeated at senior level this weekend.

Wales have lost 34 successive games in a streak of misery that goes back to 1953, including the agonising one-point loss in 2004 when Llewellyn's father Gareth was in the second row.

Last Saturday's unconvincing 28-21 win against Japan did little to raise hopes of a huge upset, but the centre stresses there is not a defeatist mindset in the Welsh camp.

Llewellyn said: "There's always the belief, especially when you come into work and you are in this Welsh jersey, that you can win.

"We are always willing to deliver everything we can, and above, to make that happen.

"We have been working really hard to make our performances more consistent and better. If we can do that then we will be in a really good spot to be a lot more competitive on Saturday."

Listen live on BBC Radio Wales, BBC Radio Cymru and BBC Radio 5Live

Llewellyn was paired with Scarlets' James, 6ft 4in, for the first time against Japan.

It was Steve Tandy's sixth different centre partnership and signalled a move away from Wales' policy of fielding a ball-player in either Joe Hawkins or Ben Thomas in midfield.

"I really enjoyed it. It was the first that I have played with Eddie and I thought we played pretty well together," said Llewellyn.

"The first week of training was about making sure we had the combination locked down and I felt that happened really quickly."

Llewellyn has had 12 on his back just once for Gloucester this season and his only previous start at inside centre for Wales was against England in a World Cup warm-up game in August 2023.

It is where the former Cardiff back sees his long-term future.

He said: "The roles are definitely different. At 12 you get a lot more direct tackles and at 13 you get a few more opportunities when you are out in a bit of space.

"I enjoy playing both and I am fortunate that I can play both, but in the long-term 12 is where I will probably be.

"I think that is where I could get the best out of myself going forward. I enjoy both positions, and they both have different opportunities, but the physical aspect of the game at 12 suits me."

articles.title: Ellie Kildunne: It's 'harsh' to say England dropped me after Canada defeat - 'My role just changed'
articles.summary: Ellie Kildunne speaks to media for the first time since being moved to the bench on the Red Roses’ North America tour; following England’s first defeat in 41 Tests against Canada, she stayed among replacements for the second Test as the Red Roses suffered consecutive defeats
articles.body:
The 27-year-old, who was named 2024's World Player of the Year and finished second to Rory McIlroy as 2025's BBC Sports Personality of the Year, played a starring role as the Red Roses clinched World Cup glory on home soil last year.

But during 2026's Global WXV series, full-back Kildunne was dropped from the starting side following defeat to Canada in Toronto - a first Red Roses loss for four years and 41 Tests.

Head coach John Mitchell revealed at the time Kildunne was "going through a difficult period" in the search for consistency.

Despite the Red Roses losing again to Canada in Ottawa, Kildunne remained on the bench for England's closing Test and emphatic victory over the USA.

"I think the word 'dropped' is probably a bit harsh," Kildunne said on Wednesday. "I still played the game, I was still part of the team, I still came on the pitch, so in no way have I been dropped. I've just been given a different role.

"Of course, finding depth in the team is very important and I've been fortunate to play a lot of rugby and have a lot of minutes under my belt.

"People are going to say whatever they want to say because everyone wants a headline and everyone wants the clickbait that they're going to read.

"I saw 'Kildunne's been dropped' and I was like: 'I'm still in America, so obviously I've not been dropped'."

Upon removing her from the starting side last month, Mitchell highlighted form, consistency and behaviours.

He said: "Well, firstly it's undisputed that she adds huge value. She's just going through a difficult period at the moment. It's important for us to help her through that.

"She wants to become consistent as well and she'll get back. It's also important to create competition and to recognise that you have to become more consistent, especially when you're competing in the Red Roses.

"So it's really important to reinforce the behaviours that we think are necessary to our game. And that goes for everyone."

For Kildunne, who will make her debut for Bristol Bears in the Premiership Women's Rugby next week following an acrimonious departure from Harlequins, she says her main learning from 2026 is to "block out the noise."

"What's really been a learning point from the tour, away from rugby, is being able to block out that noise," she said. "I've been so used to the positive comments throughout my career and as soon as you don't score one try, people seem to be against you.

"I want to be a consistent player and that might not always look like scoring. Whether for the past few years I've consistently scored, it doesn't mean that I've played badly if I haven't scored.

"That's what people have seen and rated me on: the line-breaks and the tries, but the game doesn't work like that. Everyone's evolving and getting better.

"I'm happy with my performances this year. I've had to learn a lot as a player and work out a lot. Ultimately, I don't get the space that I once had so I can't always make the 60-metre line breaks.

"I think I'm very good at balancing what I'm doing, whether it's media or training and how to do them. But I guess from the outside, people always think that you don't have the balance right.

"I think as long as you know that you're a rugby player and that's the thing that you need to focus on and you're true to that, then there should be never anything to question. But I feel like externals love to find something that could potentially be wrong.

"I've probably had that period of working it out and I'm definitely in a space now where you do have to say no to things."

articles.title: Eddie Jones: Former England coach says Japan aiming to 'make Twickenham sky fall in on' Steve Borthwick's 'distracted' charges
articles.summary: Eddie Jones, who coached England between 2016 and 2022, is now in charge of Japan for second time, with Brave Blossoms facing England at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham on Saturday (4.40pm kick-off); Jones tells BBC his Japan are aiming to 'make Twickenham sky fall in' on 'distracted' England
articles.body:
Jones, who oversaw England between 2016 and 2022, before being dismissed a year before the 2023 Rugby World Cup in France after a calendar year saw just five victories and England fans booing the side following defeat to South Africa.

The 66-year-old has since returned to Australia for an ill-fated and short second reign which ended in a first-ever World Cup pool stage exit for the Wallabies, and then returned as Japan head coach in 2024.

Ahead of his Brave Blossoms side facing England at Twickenham on Saturday, Jones has sought to stoke the flames.

"We're massive underdogs," Jones told the BBC. "We've got to find a way to disrupt an England side that's looking at New Zealand next week [Saturday November 21] and sometimes may be a little bit distracted.

"Our opportunity is to get in there, cause some havoc, cause some chaos, put off their game, get the crowd booing. Then the sky starts to come in on Twickenham and you never know what can happen.

"We've seen it happen with Italy and other countries [Italians beat England for first time in March].

"The noise does get to the team and it can be pretty loud in England. You've got a lot of newspapers, a lot of media, probably more than any other country in the world.

"Sometimes that can weigh down on the players and it's the job of the leadership to get the players thinking straight.

"Steve [Borthwick] is an outstanding coach and a very intelligent man, and a really good coach. So I've got the highest respect for him."

Jones plays down Pollock's impact on the wing - 'Wouldn't read much into it'

England are entering Saturday's Test off the back of a much-needed, morale-boosting 45-22 victory over Australia in the Nations Championship.

In a week when Borthwick came under intense scrutiny following newspaper reports of a summer rift with his England squad - claims denied by Jamie George to Sky Sports - England responded with a seven-try performance and record point haul against Australia.

Back-row Henry Pollock also starred out of position on the wing for 40 minutes, having emerged at half-time to score two tries en route to victory.

Jones was quick to play down Pollock's exploits, however.

"I wouldn't look too much into it," Jones added. "Everyone was licking the ice cream on Sunday. They were on the front foot, everyone's lining up to run the ball, there's no pressure in the game.

"He's a fast back-rower, he got the ball in space and he's a talented player, there's no doubt about it, but you couldn't read into it any more than that."
